newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Genetically altered crops seen helping Asia.
newsitem.headline: Genetically altered crops seen helping Asia.

text.p: Advances in plant biotechnology could increase crop production and open new markets for agricultural exporters such Indonesia and Malaysia, an expert said on Tuesday.
New products could be derived from commodities such as palm oil and rubber, major crops in Indonesia, said Nam-Hai Chua.
Chua, head of the laboratory of plant and molecular biology at the Rockefeller University in the United States, was speaking at an international conference on food in Jakarta.
He said rubber could be used in biodegradable plastics and pharmaceutical items while new uses for palm oil included an oil similar to olive oil.
Indonesia is the world's largest producer of palm oil after neighbouring Malaysia. Indonesia is also a leading producer of rubber, coffee, cocoa and tea.

Palm oil is used to make cooking oil, soaps and detergents, cosmetics and fabric softeners. Rubber is used to make tyres and a variety of other products including anti-earthquake cushions in high-rise buildings.
Christian Mol, president-director of PT Rabobank Dua Indonesia, said biotechnology held out exciting prospects in raising crop yields, especially in countries such as Indonesia.
"The trigger word is yield. Yields here are still low. The rice problem should not necessarily have to be solved by an extra one million hectares in Kalimantan," he said.
He was referring to the government's plan to turn one million hectares (2.5 million acres) of peat land into a giant rice farm in a bid to sustain the country's self-sufficiency in rice.
"By increasing yield, the same results can be achieved," he added.
Mol said, however, possible chain reactions that could be triggered by genetically modified crops scared him.

"It is an intriguing thought...while you try to increase the yield of a certain crop that has a consequence on related products," he said when asked what impact farming improved strains would have on global demand and supply of food items.
"It's very hard to see the consequences," he told Reuters.
He said acceptance of genetically modified crops would be easier in Asia -- compared with Europe or the United States -- where the focus is on higher yields and food security.
Chua said developments in biotechnology included rice that was bacteria-resistant and vegetables with longer shelf-lives.
"Pests have been a major problem, contributing 15-20 percent loss in crops," he said.
He said industries worldwide spent $32 billion last year on herbicides, insecticides and other chemicals.
Chua said farmers using genetically modified cotton in the United States saw a significant drop in their insecticide and related costs such as labour while reducing health hazards.
He said rice plants containing genes taken from wild rice were found to be resistant to bacteria while biotechnology has been used to increase the starch content in potatoes.
